claim: Standard economic theory fails to account for choice biases.
source: Standard economic theory fails to account for these effects, and shedding light on their origins is a long-term goal for neuroeconomics (Camerer et al., 2005; Glimcher and Rustichini, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The neural underpinnings of simple choices were poorly understood until recently.
source: Progress on this front has been relatively modest, largely because the neural underpinnings of (even simple) choices were poorly understood until recently.
evidence: This is a historical assessment of the field.

claim: The last 15 years have witnessed substantial advances in understanding neural underpinnings of choices.
source: However, the last 15 years have witnessed substantial advances.
evidence: This is a historical assessment of recent progress in the field.

claim: An important turning point was the development of experimental protocols in which subjects choose between different goods and relative subjective values are inferred from choices.
source: An important turning point was the development of experimental protocols in which subjects choose between different goods and relative subjective values are inferred from choices.
evidence: This describes a methodological advance in the field.

claim: Decision variables defined from subjective values are used to interpret neural activity.
source: Decision variables defined from these values are used to interpret neural activity (Kable and Glimcher, 2007; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Plassmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This methodological approach is supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in numerous brain regions represent the values of offered and chosen goods.
source: Studies that adopted this paradigm showed that neurons in numerous brain regions represent the values of offered and chosen goods (Amemori and Graybiel, 2012; Cai et al., 2011; Cai and Padoa-Schioppa, 2012; Hosokawa et al., 2013; Jezzini and Padoa-Schioppa, 2020; Kim et al., 2008; Lak et al., 2014; Levy et al., 2010; Louie and Glimcher, 2010; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Pastor-Bernier et al., 2019; Shenhav and Greene, 2010).
evidence: This finding is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Offer values encoded in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) are causally linked to choices.
source: Furthermore, recent experiments using electrical stimulation showed that offer values encoded in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) are causally linked to choices (Ballesta et al., 2020).
evidence: This causal claim is supported by a citation to an electrical stimulation study.

claim: The identification of distinct groups of neurons encoding different decision variables in OFC and other brain regions is essential to ultimately understand the neural circuit and mechanisms through which economic decisions are formed.
source: First, the identification in OFC and other brain regions of distinct groups of neurons encoding different decision variables is essential to ultimately understand the neural circuit and the mechanisms through which economic decisions are formed.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings for understanding neural circuits.

claim: Neuronal firing rates in brain regions being linearly related to values defined behaviorally constitutes powerful evidence that choices indeed entail the computation of values.
source: In this perspective, the fact that neuronal firing rates in any brain region are linearly related to values defined at the behavioral level constitutes powerful evidence that choices indeed entail the computation of values (Camerer, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of neural value encoding, supported by a citation.

claim: The construct of value suffers from a fundamental problem of circularity at the behavioral level.
source: Although this idea has remained influential, values defined at the behavioral level suffer from a fundamental problem of circularity. On the one hand, choices supposedly maximize values; on the other hand, values cannot be measured behaviorally independent of choices (Samuelson, 1938).
evidence: This is a well-known conceptual problem in economics, supported by a citation.

claim: The construct of value gradually lost centrality in economic theory because of the circularity problem.
source: Because of this problem, the construct of value gradually lost centrality in economic theory.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the development of economic theory.

claim: In standard neoclassic formulation, choices are 'as if' driven by values, but there is no commitment to the idea that agents actually compute values.
source: Thus, in the standard neoclassic formulation choices are 'as if' driven by values, but there is no commitment to the idea that agents actually compute values (Samuelson, 1947).
evidence: This describes the standard economic approach, supported by a citation.

claim: The identification of neurons encoding offer values and other decision variables provides the opportunity to break the circularity problem.
source: Third and less frequently discussed, the identification of neurons encoding offer values and other decision variables, together with some rudimentary understanding of the decision circuit, provides the opportunity to break the circularity problem described above.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about how neuroscience can address a fundamental problem in economics.

claim: People and monkeys typically show a bias favoring the second option when choosing between two options offered sequentially.
source: For example, while choosing between two options offered sequentially, people and monkeys typically show a bias favoring the second option (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019; Krajbich et al., 2010; Rustichini et al., 2021).
evidence: This behavioral phenomenon is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The order bias might occur because subjects assign a higher value to any given good if that good is offered second.
source: This order bias might occur for at least two reasons. (1) Subjects might assign a higher value to any given good if that good is offered second.
evidence: This is a hypothetical explanation for the order bias.

claim: The order bias might occur because subjects assign identical values independent of the presentation order, and the bias emerges downstream of valuation during value comparison.
source: (2) Alternatively, subjects might assign identical values independent of the presentation order, and the bias might emerge downstream of valuation, for example during value comparison.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothetical explanation for the order bias.

claim: If the order bias emerges downstream of valuation, the decision process would fail to maximize the value obtained by the agent.
source: In the latter scenario, by introducing the order bias, the decision process would actually fail to maximize the value obtained by the agent.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the second hypothesis about the order bias.

claim: The two hypotheses about the order bias are not distinguishable based on behavior alone due to the circularity problem.
source: Due to the circularity problem described above, these two hypotheses are ultimately not distinguishable based on behavior alone.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the circularity problem in behavioral economics.

claim: Access to a credible neural measure for the offer values makes it possible to disambiguate between the two hypotheses about the order bias.
source: However, access to a credible neural measure for the offer values makes it possible, at least in principle, to disambiguate between them.
evidence: This is a key conceptual claim about how neural data can resolve behavioral ambiguities.

claim: Monkeys chose between two juices offered in variable amounts in each session.
source: In the experiments, monkeys chose between two juices offered in variable amounts.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

source: In each session, we randomly interleaved two types of trials referred to as two tasks.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

source: In Task 1, offers were presented simultaneously

claim: In Task 2, offers were presented in sequence.
source: in Task 2, offers were presented in sequence.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for Task 2.

evidence: This is a primary behavioral finding from comparing the two tasks.

claim: Choices in Task 2 were biased in favor of the second offer (order bias).
source: (2) Choices in Task 2 were biased in favor of the second offer (order bias).

claim: Choices in Task 2 were biased in favor of the preferred juice (preference bias).
source: (3) Choices in Task 2 were biased in favor of the preferred juice (preference bias).

claim: In most daily situations, offers available for choice appear or are examined sequentially.

claim: Neuronal recordings focused on the OFC.
source: Neuronal recordings focused on the OFC.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Earlier work identified different groups of cells in OFC encoding individual offer values, the binary choice outcome (chosen juice), and the chosen value.
source: Earlier work on choices under simultaneous offers identified in this area different groups of cells encoding individual offer values, the binary choice outcome (chosen juice), and the chosen value (Padoa-Schioppa, 2013; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).

claim: Choices under sequential offers engage the same neuronal populations as choices under simultaneous offers.
source: Furthermore, previous analyses indicated that choices under sequential offers engage the same neuronal populations (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019; Shi et al., 2022a).
evidence: This finding is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cell groups labeled offer value, chosen juice and chosen value can be identified in either choice task and appear to preserve their functional role.

source: In first approximation, the variables encoded in OFC capture both the input (offer values) and the output (chosen juice, chosen value) of the choice process

source: suggesting that the cell groups identified in this area constitute the building blocks of a decision circuit (Padoa-Schioppa and Conen, 2017).

source: A series of experimental (Ballesta et al., 2021; Camille et al., 2011; Rich and Wallis, 2016) and theoretical (Friedrich and Lengyel, 2016; Rustichini and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015; Solway and Botvinick, 2012; Song et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018) results support this view.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Different groups of OFC neurons participate in value computation and value comparison.
source: In our account, different groups of OFC neurons participate in value computation and value comparison
evidence: This is part of the computational framework proposed by the authors.

claim: Value computation and value comparison are embedded in an ensemble of mental operations taking place before, during, and after the decision itself.
source: and these processes are embedded in an ensemble of mental operations taking place before, during, and after the decision itself.
evidence: This is part of the computational framework proposed by the authors.

claim: Sensory information, memory traces, and internal states are processed upstream of OFC and integrated in the activity of offer value cells.
source: In this view, sensory information, memory traces, and internal states are processed upstream of OFC and integrated in the activity of offer value cells.
evidence: This is part of the computational framework proposed by the authors, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The order bias and the preference bias highlighted significant differences between neuronal and behavioral measures of value.
source: Thus, the order bias and the preference bias highlighted significant differences between neuronal and behavioral measures of value.

claim: The three behavioral phenomena described were detrimental to the animals.

claim: The preference bias affected choices in Task 2 rather than Task 1.
source: With respect to the preference bias, one question is whether the bias affected choices in Task 1 or in Task 2 (in principle, there could be a bias favoring the unpreferred juice in Task 1). The fact that ρbehavioralTask1, ρneuronalTask1, and ρneuronalTask2 were all indistinguishable from each other while ρbehavioralTask2 differed from them (Figure 7) argues for the latter understanding.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing multiple measures of relative value across tasks, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: The putative metabolic cost of increasing performance in the task did not explicitly enter the decision process.

source: For Task 1 (simultaneous offers), the probit fit provided measures for the relative value ρTask1 and the sigmoid steepness ηTask1.
evidence: This describes the behavioral measures derived from Task 1.

claim: For Task 2, the probit fit provided measures for the relative value ρTask2, the sigmoid steepness ηTask2, and the order bias ε.
source: For Task 2 (sequential offers), the probit fit provided measures for the relative value ρTask2, the sigmoid steepness ηTask2, and the order bias ε.
evidence: This describes the behavioral measures derived from Task 2.

claim: Log value ratio models provided a better fit compared to value difference models.
source: We generally found that log value ratio models provided a better fit compared to value difference models, consistent with theoretical considerations (Padoa-Schioppa, 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses, supported by a citation.

claim: Logit models provided a better fit compared to probit models.
source: We also found that logit models provided a better fit compared to probit models
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses.

claim: Measures of relative value, sigmoid steepness, and order bias were very similar and highly correlated between logit and probit models.
source: although measures of relative value, sigmoid steepness, and order bias were very similar and highly correlated.
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses comparing different models.

claim: Both choice tasks engage the same groups of neurons in OFC.
source: The present analyses build on the results of a previous study showing that both choice tasks engage the same groups of neurons in OFC (Shi et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is a key finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: The original data set included 1526 neurons (672 from monkey J, 854 from monkey G) recorded in 306 sessions (115 from monkey J, 191 from monkey G).
source: The original data set included 1526 neurons (672 from monkey J, 854 from monkey G) recorded in 306 sessions (115 from monkey J, 191 from monkey G).
evidence: This describes the size of the original data set.

claim: For Task 1, four time windows were defined: post-offer (0.5 s after offer onset), late-delay (0.5–1 s after offer onset), pre-juice (0.5 s before juice onset), and post-juice (0.5 s after juice onset).
source: For Task 1, we defined four time windows: post-offer (0.5 s after offer onset), late-delay (0.5–1 s after offer onset), pre-juice (0.5 s before juice onset), and post-juice (0.5 s after juice onset).
evidence: This describes the time windows used for analysis in Task 1.

claim: For Task 2, three time windows were defined: post-offer1 (0.5 s after offer1 onset), post-offer2 (0.5 s after offer2 onset) and post-juice (0.5 s after juice onset).
source: For Task 2, we defined three time windows: post-offer1 (0.5 s after offer1 onset), post-offer2 (0.5 s after offer2 onset) and post-juice (0.5 s after juice onset).
evidence: This describes the time windows used for analysis in Task 2.

claim: Neurons passing the p < 0.01 criterion in ≥1 time window in either task were identified as 'task-related' and included in subsequent analyses.
source: Neurons passing the p < 0.01 criterion in ≥1 time window in either task were identified as 'task-related' and included in subsequent analyses.
evidence: This describes the criterion for including neurons in the analysis.

claim: Neurons in Task 1 were classified in one of four groups: offer value A, offer value B, chosen juice, or chosen value.
source: Following earlier work (Padoa-Schioppa, 2013), neurons in Task 1 were classified in one of four groups offer value A, offer value B, chosen juice, or chosen value.
evidence: This describes the classification scheme for Task 1, based on earlier work.

claim: Each variable could be encoded with positive or negative sign, leading to a total of eight cell groups in Task 1.
source: Each variable could be encoded with positive or negative sign, leading to a total of eight cell groups.
evidence: This describes the classification scheme for Task 1.

claim: Under sequential offers, neuronal responses in OFC were found to encode different variables defined in relation to the presentation order (AB or BA).
source: Under sequential offers, neuronal responses in OFC were found to encode different variables defined in relation to the presentation order (AB or BA).
evidence: This describes a key finding about neuronal encoding in Task 2.

claim: The vast majority of neuronal responses in Task 2 were explained by one of 11 variables.
source: Specifically, the vast majority of responses were explained by one of 11 variables including 1 binary variable capturing the presentation order (AB | BA), 6 variables representing individual offer values (offer value A | AB, offer value A | BA, offer value B | AB, offer value B | BA, offer value 1, and offer value 2), 3 variables capturing variants of the chosen value (chosen value, chosen value A, and chosen value B), and a binary variable representing the binary choice outcome (chosen juice).
evidence: This describes the variables encoded by neurons in Task 2.

claim: Most neurons encoded different variables in different time windows in Task 2.
source: Most neurons encoded different variables in different time windows.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of neuronal encoding in Task 2.

claim: The vast majority of neurons presented one of eight patterns referred to as 'sequences' in Task 2.
source: However, the vast majority of neurons presented one of eight patterns referred to as 'sequences'.
evidence: This describes the classification scheme for Task 2.

claim: A strong correspondence was found between the cell classes identified in the two choice tasks.
source: In essence, we found a strong correspondence between the cell classes identified in the two choice tasks (Shi et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is a key finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: The entire data set included 1204 neurons (577 from monkey J, 627 from monkey G) recorded in 241 sessions (101 from monkey J, 140 from monkey G).
source: Thus, our entire data set included 1204 neurons (577 from monkey J, 627 from monkey G) recorded in 241 sessions (101 from monkey J, 140 from monkey G).
evidence: This describes the size of the final data set after applying inclusion criteria.

claim: The classification procedures identified 183 offer value cells, 160 chosen juice cells, and 174 chosen value cells in the primary data set.
source: In this population, the classification procedures identified 183 offer value cells, 160 chosen juice cells, and 174 chosen value cells.
evidence: This describes the composition of the primary data set.

claim: An additional data set was recorded from the same two animals performing only Task 2.
source: However, some analyses included only trials from Task 2 and quantified the effects due to the presentation order (AB vs. BA). In these analyses, we included an additional data set recorded previously from the same two animals performing only Task 2 (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019).
evidence: This describes an additional data set used for some analyses, supported by a citation.

claim: The additional data set included 1205 neurons (414 from monkey J, 791 from monkey G) recorded in 196 sessions (51 from monkey J, 145 from monkey G).
source: The resulting data set included 1205 neurons (414 from monkey J, 791 from monkey G) recorded in 196 sessions (51 from monkey J, 145 from monkey G).
evidence: This describes the size of the additional data set.

claim: The classification procedures identified 243 offer value cells, 182 chosen juice cells, and 187 chosen value cells in the additional data set.
source: In this population, the classification procedures identified 243 offer value cells, 182 chosen juice cells, and 187 chosen value cells.
evidence: This describes the composition of the additional data set.

claim: The order bias was also observed in the sessions from the additional data set.
source: Importantly, the order bias was also observed in these sessions (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019).
evidence: This confirms that the order bias was present in the additional data set, supported by a citation.

claim: Positive and negative encoding corresponded to b1 > 0 and b1 < 0, respectively.
source: Positive and negative encoding corresponded to b1 > 0 and b1 < 0, respectively.
evidence: This defines the sign of neuronal encoding.

claim: The mean activity was defined as rmean = b0 + b1Smax/2.
source: Indicating with Smax the maximum value of S, the mean activity was defined as rmean = b0 + b1Smax/2.
evidence: This defines a measure of neuronal activity.

claim: The activity range was defined as Δr = |b1Smax|.
source: The activity range was defined as Δr = |b1Smax|, where |·| indicates the absolute value.
evidence: This defines a measure of neuronal activity range.

claim: In Task 1, chosen value cells encode the chosen value independently of the juice type.
source: In Task 1, these neurons encode the chosen value independently of the juice type.
evidence: This describes the encoding property of chosen value cells in Task 1.

claim: The neuronal measure of relative value (ρneuronal) is statistically indistinguishable from the behavioral measure (ρbehavioral) derived from the probit analysis of choice patterns.
source: Previous studies showed that this measure is statistically indistinguishable from the behavioral measure ρbehavioral derived from the probit analysis of choice patterns (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by a citation.

claim: In Task 2, in the post-offer1 and post-offer2 time windows, chosen value cells encoded the value of the current offer, independent of the juice type.
source: In Task 2, in the post-offer1 and post-offer2 time windows, chosen value cells encoded the value of the current offer, independent of the juice type (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the encoding property of chosen value cells in Task 2, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The activity of chosen juice cells in OE trials shortly before offer2 is inversely related to the value of offer1.
source: We previously showed that the activity of these neurons recorded in OE trials shortly before offer2 is inversely related to the value of offer1 (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Circuit inhibition resembles the setting of a dynamic system's initial conditions and is regarded as an integral part of the decision process.
source: This phenomenon, termed circuit inhibition, resembles the setting of a dynamic system's initial conditions and is regarded as an integral part of the decision process (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of circuit inhibition, supported by a citation.

claim: Offer value signals in Task 2 were significantly weaker than in Task 1.
source: Comparing neuronal responses across tasks, we noted that offer value signals in Task 2 were significantly weaker than in Task 1.
evidence: This is a primary neuronal finding comparing the two tasks.

claim: At the population level, the mean activity of offer value cells did not differ significantly across tasks.
source: At the population level, the mean activity did not differ significantly across tasks (p = 0.6, t-test; p = 0.4, Wilcoxon test, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a population-level finding, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The activity range of offer value cells was significantly lower in Task 2 compared to Task 1.
source: In contrast, the activity range was significantly lower in Task 2 compared to Task 1 (ΔrTask2 < ΔrTask1; p = 0.06, t-test; p = 0.02, Wilcoxon test Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a population-level finding, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The activity of offer value cells is causally related to choices.
source: The activity of offer value cells is causally related to choices (Ballesta et al., 2020).
evidence: This causal claim is supported by a citation to an electrical stimulation study.

claim: Decreases in the encoding slope of offer value cells due to range adaptation reduce choice accuracy.
source: Indeed, we previously found that decreases in the encoding slope of offer value cells due to range adaptation reduce choice accuracy (Conen and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019; Rustichini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The difference in sigmoid steepness (Δη) and the difference in activity range (Δr) of offer value cells were positively correlated.
source: The two measures were positively correlated (Spearman r = 0.2, p = 0.01; Pearson r = 0.3, p = 0.003; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a key finding linking neuronal and behavioral measures, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The drop in choice accuracy observed in Task 2 compared to Task 1 correlated with weaker offer value signals in OFC.
source: In other words, the drop in choice accuracy observed in Task 2 compared to Task 1 correlated with weaker offer value signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between Δη and Δr.

claim: The activity range of chosen value cells was reduced in Task 2 compared to Task 1, but this effect did not correlate with the drop in choice accuracy.
source: A similar analysis of chosen value cells found that the activity range Δr was reduced in Task 2 compared to Task 1. However, this effect and the drop in choice accuracy were not significantly correlated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from an analysis of chosen value cells, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lower choice accuracy measured in Task 2 compared to Task 1 correlated with weaker offer value signals in OFC, indicating this behavioral phenomenon emerged at least partly during valuation.
source: In conclusion, the lower choice accuracy measured in Task 2 compared to Task 1 correlated with weaker offer value signals in OFC. Thus, this behavioral phenomenon emerged, at least partly, during valuation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses of offer value cells.

claim: Across a population of 128 offer value cells, there was no systematic difference in mean activity or activity range between EO trials (post-offer1) and OE trials (post-offer2).
source: Contrary to this prediction, across a population of 128 cells, we did not find any systematic difference in mean activity or activity range (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of offer value cells, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference between the activity parameters measured in OE and EO trials did not correlate with the order bias.
source: Furthermore, the difference between the activity parameters measured in OE and EO trials did not correlate with the order bias (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of offer value cells, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Assigned values did not depend on the presentation order.
source: In conclusion, assigned values did not depend on the presentation order.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of offer value cells.

claim: The neuronal measures ρneuronalAB and ρneuronalBA were correlated with each other.
source: Similarly, the two neuronal measures of relative value, ρneuronalAB and ρneuronalBA, were correlated with each other (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of chosen value cells, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The difference Δρneuronal and the order bias ε were significantly correlated across the population of chosen value cells.
source: Most importantly, the difference Δρneuronal and the order bias ε were significantly correlated across the population (Spearman r = 0.3, p = 0.007; Pearson r = 0.2, p = 0.02; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a key finding linking neuronal and behavioral measures, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Session-to-session fluctuations in the activity of chosen value cells correlated with fluctuations in the order bias.
source: Hence, session-to-session fluctuations in the activity of chosen value cells correlated with fluctuations in the order bias.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between Δρneuronal and ε.

claim: The baseline activity of chosen juice cells recorded in OE trials immediately before offer2 was negatively correlated with the value of offer1.
source: A previous study found that the baseline activity of chosen juice cells recorded in OE trials immediately before offer2 was negatively correlated with the value of offer1 (i.e., the value of the other juice) – a phenomenon termed circuit inhibition (Ballesta and Padoa-Schioppa, 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Circuit inhibition sets the system's initial conditions and is integral to value comparison.
source: If the decision is conceptualized as the evolution of a dynamic system (Rustichini and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015; Wang, 2002), circuit inhibition sets the system's initial conditions and is thus integral to value comparison.
evidence: This is an interpretation of circuit inhibition, supported by citations.

claim: The intensity of circuit inhibition should be negatively correlated with the order bias.
source: If so, the intensity of circuit inhibition should be negatively correlated with the order bias.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the interpretation of circuit inhibition.

claim: Across a population of 295 chosen juice cells, mean(c1) was significantly <0, confirming the presence of circuit inhibition.
source: Across a population of 295 chosen juice cells, mean(c1) was significantly <0 (p = 5 × 10−6, t-test; p = 9 × 10−8, Wilcoxon test; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding confirming circuit inhibition, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Circuit inhibition (c1) and the order bias (ε) were significantly correlated across the population of chosen juice cells.
source: Confirming the prediction, the two measures were significantly correlated across the population (Spearman r = 0.1, p = 0.02; Pearson r = 0.1, p = 0.02; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a key finding linking circuit inhibition to the order bias, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Stronger circuit inhibition (more negative c1) corresponded to a weaker order bias (smaller ε).
source: In other words, stronger circuit inhibition (more negative c1) corresponded to a weaker order bias (smaller ε).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between c1 and ε.

claim: The order bias did not originate before or during valuation.
source: In conclusion, the order bias did not originate before or during valuation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of offer value cells.

claim: Analysis of chosen juice cells and chosen value cells indicated that the order bias emerged during value comparison (decision stage).
source: Analysis of chosen juice cells and chosen value cells indicated that the order bias emerged during value comparison (decision stage).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses of chosen juice and chosen value cells.

claim: The preference bias did not emerge during valuation.
source: Contrary to the prediction, we did not find any correlation between neuronal measures (Δb0, Δb1) and the behavioral measure (ρ) for either offer value A or offer value B cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). Thus, the preference bias did not seem to emerge at the valuation stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of offer value cells, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ρneuronalTask2 was statistically indistinguishable from ρbehavioralTask1 and systematically smaller than ρbehavioralTask2.
source: In essence, ρneuronalTask2 was statistically indistinguishable from ρbehavioralTask1 and systematically lower than ρbehavioralTask2.
evidence: This is a key finding from the analysis of chosen value cells, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The chosen value represented in the brain in Task 2 was equal to that inferred from choices in Task 1, and significantly different from that inferred from choices in Task 2.
source: This result is quite remarkable. It shows that the chosen value represented in the brain in Task 2 was equal to that inferred from choices in Task 1, and significantly different from that inferred from choices in Task 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding about ρneuronal measures.

claim: The preference bias was costly for the monkey, as it reduced the value obtained on average at the end of each trial.
source: This fact implies that the preference bias was costly for the monkey, as it reduced the value obtained on average at the end of each trial (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference from the discrepancy between neuronal and behavioral values.

claim: The preference bias did not reflect differences in the values assigned to individual offers (offer values).
source: In summary, the preference bias did not reflect differences in the values assigned to individual offers (offer values).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of offer value cells.

claim: Insofar as the activity of chosen value cells reflects the decision process, the preference bias did not seem to emerge during value comparison.
source: Furthermore, insofar as the activity of chosen value cells reflects the decision process (Figure 1), the preference bias did not seem to emerge during value comparison.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of chosen value cells, in the context of the framework shown in Figure 1.

claim: The preference bias might be due to the higher demands of Task 2, where if the animal had not finalized its decision or failed to retain the decision outcome in working memory, it might have selected the target associated with the better juice (juice A).
source: At the cognitive level, the preference bias might be interpreted as due to the higher demands of Task 2. When the two saccade targets appeared on the monitor, information about values was no longer on display (Figure 2B). If at that point the animal had not finalized its decision, or if it had failed to retain in working memory the decision outcome, the animal might have selected the target associated with the better juice (juice A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the preference bias, in the context of Figure 2B.

claim: The preference bias would have been especially strong when the value difference between the two juices was large.
source: Such bias would have been especially strong when the value difference between the two juices was large.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the speculative interpretation of the preference bias.

claim: The preference bias would reflect a 'second thought' occurring after value comparison, in some trials.
source: In this view, the preference bias would reflect a 'second thought' occurring after value comparison, in some trials.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the preference bias.

claim: The evolving decision in Task 2 was captured by the activity of chosen juice cells recorded in OE trials immediately before and after offer2 onset.
source: As noted above, in Task 2, the evolving decision was captured by the activity of these neurons recorded in OE trials immediately before and after offer2 onset (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of chosen juice cell activity, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The state of the ongoing decision was captured by the distance between the two traces corresponding to the two possible choice outcomes (E chosen, O chosen).
source: More specifically, the state of the ongoing decision was captured by the distance between the two traces corresponding to the two possible choice outcomes (E chosen, O chosen).
evidence: This is a statement about how the decision state is quantified from neuronal activity.

claim: Across the population of chosen juice cells, mean(CP) exceeded chance level starting shortly before offer2.
source: Across the population, mean(CP) exceeded chance level starting shortly before offer2, consistent with the above discussion on circuit inhibition.
evidence: This is a finding from the ROC analysis of chosen juice cells.

claim: The intensity of the preference bias should be inversely related to the animals' commitment to the eventual choice outcome measured earlier in the trial.
source: If the preference bias emerged late in the trial – perhaps after target presentation, if animals had not already finalized their decision – the intensity of the preference bias should be inversely related to the animals' commitment to the eventual choice outcome measured earlier in the trial.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis that the preference bias emerges late in the trial.

claim: There should be a negative correlation between the preference bias and CPs computed at the time when decisions normally take place (shortly before or after offer2 onset).
source: In other words, there should be a negative correlation between the preference bias and CPs computed at the time when decisions normally take place (shortly before or after offer2 onset).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis that the preference bias emerges late in the trial.

claim: CP and PBI were significantly anti-correlated immediately before and during offer2 presentation, but not in the control time window or late in the trial.
source: Confirming our predictions, CP and PBI were significantly anti-correlated immediately before and during offer2 presentation, but not in the control time window or late in the trial (Figure 8F–I).
evidence: This is a key finding supporting the hypothesis that the preference bias emerges late in the trial, shown in Figure 8F–I.

claim: The results suggest that the preference bias emerged late in the trial, as a 'second thought' process that guided choices when decisions were not finalized based on offer values alone.
source: In conclusion, our results indicated that the preference bias did not emerge during valuation or during value comparison. Conversely, our results suggest that the preference bias emerged late in the trial, as a 'second thought' process that guided choices when decisions were not finalized based on offer values alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses of chosen juice cells.

claim: The proposal that choices entail computing and comparing subjective values was put forth by early economists such as Bernoulli and Bentham.
source: The proposal that choices entail computing and comparing subjective values was put forth by early economists such as Bernoulli and Bentham (Niehans, 1990).
evidence: This is a historical statement about economic theory, supported by a citation.

claim: Values defined at the behavioral level suffer from a fundamental problem of circularity: choices supposedly maximize values, but values cannot be measured behaviorally independent of choices.
source: Although this idea has remained influential, values defined at the behavioral level suffer from a fundamental problem of circularity. On the one hand, choices supposedly maximize values; on the other hand, values cannot be measured behaviorally independent of choices (Samuelson, 1938).
evidence: This is a well-known conceptual problem in economics, supported by a citation.

claim: Neuroscience results showing that neuronal activity in multiple brain regions is linearly related to values defined behaviorally constitute a significant breakthrough.
source: In this perspective, neuroscience results showing that neuronal activity in multiple brain regions is linearly related to values defined behaviorally (Amemori and Graybiel, 2012; Cai et al., 2011; Cai and Padoa-Schioppa, 2012; Hosokawa et al., 2013; Jezzini and Padoa-Schioppa, 2020; Kable and Glimcher, 2007; Kim et al., 2008; Lak et al., 2014; Levy et al., 2010; Louie and Glimcher, 2010; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Pastor-Bernier et al., 2019; Plassmann et al., 2007; Shenhav and Greene, 2010), constitute a significant breakthrough.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of neuroscience findings, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neuroscience results validate the concept of value and effectively break the circularity surrounding it.
source: They validate the concept of value and effectively break the circularity surrounding it.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of neuroscience findings for economic theory.

claim: A neuronal population whose activity is reliably correlated with values measured from choices may be used to derive independent measures of subjective values.
source: Indeed, a neuronal population whose activity is reliably correlated with values measured from choices (behavioral values) may be used to derive independent measures of subjective values (neuronal values).
evidence: This is a key conceptual point about how neural data can provide independent measures of value.

claim: In most circumstances, neuronal values and behavioral values should be (and are) indistinguishable.
source: In most circumstances, neuronal values and behavioral values should be (and are) indistinguishable.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between neuronal and behavioral values.

claim: In specific choice contexts, neuronal values and behavioral values might differ somewhat.
source: However, in specific choice contexts, the two measures might differ somewhat.
evidence: This is a statement about when neuronal and behavioral values might diverge.

claim: When neuronal and behavioral values differ, such discrepancies indicate that choices are partly determined by processes that escape the maximization of offer values.
source: When observed, such discrepancies indicate that choices are partly determined by processes that escape the maximization of offer values.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what it means when neuronal and behavioral values differ.

claim: Suitable analyses of neuronal activity may be used to assess the origins of particular choice biases.
source: If so, suitable analyses of neuronal activity may be used to assess the origins of particular choice biases.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential of neural data to understand choice biases.

claim: Good-based economic decisions take place in OFC.
source: It is generally understood that good-based economic decisions take place in OFC (Cisek, 2012; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Rushworth et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a statement about the role of OFC in decision-making, supported by citations.

claim: The encoding of decision variables in OFC is categorical in nature.
source: and that the encoding of decision variables in this area is categorical in nature (Hirokawa et al., 2019; Onken et al., 2019; Padoa-Schioppa, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of neuronal encoding in OFC, supported by citations.

claim: Different cell groups in OFC may be associated with different computational stages: offer value cells instantiate the valuation stage; chosen value cells reflect values possibly modified by the decision process; and chosen juice cells capture the evolving commitment to a particular choice outcome.
source: More specifically, we hypothesize that offer value cells provide the primary input to a circuit formed by chosen juice cells and chosen value cells, where decisions are formed. In this view, different cell groups in OFC may be associated with different computational stages: offer value cells instantiate the valuation stage; chosen value cells reflect values possibly modified by the decision process; and chosen juice cells capture the evolving commitment to a particular choice outcome.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional roles of different OFC cell groups.
